--- title: "Chapter 1. Introduction to Causality" subtitle: "Potential outcomes, the fundamental problem, and selection bias" date: 2026-08-01 categories: [foundations, potential outcomes, bias] jupyter: python3 --- ## [1]{.chapter-step} The question {#sec-question} Everyone already distinguishes *association* from *causation*. Stated that way the distinction is intuitive and useless: it cannot be computed, argued with, or checked against data. This chapter makes both precise. **Association** turns out to be a statement about two *different groups* of units; **causation**, a statement about *one group* under two different treatments. Once they are written down, they are visibly different quantities — and only one of the two can be computed from data. The obstacle is that a causal claim needs an observation that does not exist: the same unit both treated and untreated. That is the {{< term fundamental-problem >}} [@holland1986]. So **causal inference is what makes a causal quantity computable anyway** — a set of assumptions under which it can be rewritten using only quantities you can observe. Every method in this course is one such set, and the rest of this chapter is the minimum notation needed to state any of them. ## [2]{.chapter-step} Intuition {#sec-intuition} Hospitals are full of sick people. Does that mean hospitals damage your health? The question sounds silly, but its structure is exactly that of most business questions. Users who installed the app spend more — does the app increase revenue? Employees who took the training perform better — is that the training, or is it that strong performers get sent to training? The problem is the same every time: **the groups differed before any treatment happened**. Comparing their outcomes adds the treatment effect to that pre-existing gap, and nothing in the comparison separates the two. This forces a shift in how the question is posed. The right question is not "how do the treated differ from the untreated". The right question is "what would have happened to **these same** people had they not been treated". The second question is about data we do not have. That is why causal inference is a discipline about recovering missing data, rather than about describing the data in hand. ## [3]{.chapter-step} Formalism {#sec-formalism} ### Potential outcomes Every unit $i$ has **two** outcomes defined: $$ \begin{aligned} Y_i(0) &\quad \text{what would happen without treatment} \\ Y_i(1) &\quad \text{what would happen with it} \end{aligned} $$ The causal effect for that unit is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. We observe only one of the two, depending on the realized assignment $T_i \in \{0, 1\}$: $$ Y_i = T_i \cdot Y_i(1) + (1 - T_i) \cdot Y_i(0). $$ ::: {.recall} The observed outcome is a **collapse** of the potential-outcome pair. The other half — the {{< term counterfactual >}} — is not merely unknown, it is unobservable in principle. This is the [fundamental problem of causal inference](/glossary.qmd#term-fundamental-problem) [@holland1986]. ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true"} ## Notation across the standard references This playbook writes $T$ for treatment and $Y(1), Y(0)$ for the potential outcomes, after @rubin1974 and @facure2022. @hernan2020 write $A$ for the treatment and $Y^{a=1}, Y^{a=0}$ for the same two objects, and call {{< term ignorability >}} *conditional exchangeability*; @angrist2009 call the same assumption the conditional independence assumption. The objects are identical and only the names differ — with one genuine exception, recorded in the {{< term selection-bias >}} glossary entry, where the two literatures attach the same words to different things. ::: ### What can actually be estimated The individual effect $\tau_i$ is never available. Averages are: $$ \begin{aligned} \text{ATE} &= \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)] \\ \text{ATT} &= \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T = 1] \\ \text{CATE}(x) &= \mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = x] \end{aligned} $$ {{< term ate >}} answers "what happens if we treat everyone". {{< term att >}} answers "what did treatment do for those who got it". Under a heterogeneous effect these are different numbers, and substituting one for the other is not a rounding error. ### Six people and one decision {#sec-example} Take the smallest example that still contains everything. Six people; three went to college ($T = 1$) and three did not ($T = 0$); $Y$ is annual income in thousands, measured ten years on. Now step outside the data and write down **both** potential outcomes for all six — the thing no dataset ever contains. Bold is what was actually observed, italic is the half that was not. | Person | $T$ | $Y(0)$ | $Y(1)$ | $\tau_i$ | |:---|:---:|---:|---:|---:| | A | 1 | *60* | **75** | 15 | | B | 1 | *55* | **68** | 13 | | C | 1 | *50* | **64** | 14 | | D | 0 | **40** | *48* | 8 | | E | 0 | **35** | *44* | 9 | | F | 0 | **30** | *37* | 7 | : Six units with both potential outcomes revealed. Exactly one number per row is ever real data; the individual effect $\tau_i$ in the last column is never computable outside a thought experiment like this one. The shape of the table follows @facure2022 [ch. 1] and @hernan2020 [ch. 1]; the numbers are invented for this page. {#tbl-units} Two things are true of @tbl-units at once, and between them they are the whole chapter. College helps **everyone** — the effect runs from 7 to 15 and is never negative. And the three who went were already the higher earners: their $Y(0)$ values are 60, 55, 50 against 40, 35, 30. Nothing caused that gap. It is simply who chose to go. Average each quadrant and one small table holds every quantity in the chapter. Hover or tab onto a cell to see what it is. ::: {.pb-tip-table} | | $T = 0$ — did not go | $T = 1$ — went | Both groups | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | **$Y(0)$**
nobody goes | [$\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=0]$]{.tip tip="Average income of the three who did not go, in the world that happened. This cell is data: it is just the mean outcome in the untreated group."}
[35]{.pb-val}[factual]{.pb-tag} | [$\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=1]$]{.tip tip="What the three who went would have earned had they not gone. Never observed. It is 55 and not 35 because these three would have out-earned the others with or without college."}
[55]{.pb-val}[counterfactual]{.pb-tag .is-cf} | [$\mathbb{E}[Y(0)]$]{.tip tip="Average income if none of the six had gone. Half the numbers behind it are counterfactual, so no dataset reports this."}
[45]{.pb-val} | | **$Y(1)$**
everybody goes | [$\mathbb{E}[Y(1) \mid T=0]$]{.tip tip="What the three who did not go would have earned had they gone. Never observed."}
[43]{.pb-val}[counterfactual]{.pb-tag .is-cf} | [$\mathbb{E}[Y(1) \mid T=1]$]{.tip tip="Average income of the three who went, in the world that happened. Also data: the mean outcome in the treated group."}
[69]{.pb-val}[factual]{.pb-tag} | [$\mathbb{E}[Y(1)]$]{.tip tip="Average income if all six had gone. The same problem in mirror image."}
[56]{.pb-val} | | **effect**
down a column | [$\text{ATU}$]{.tip tip="Average effect on the untreated: 43 minus 35. What college would have done for the three who skipped it."}
[8]{.pb-val} | [$\text{ATT}$]{.tip tip="Average effect on the treated: 69 minus 55. What college actually did for the three who went."}
[14]{.pb-val} | [$\text{ATE}$]{.tip tip="Average effect over all six: 56 minus 45. It sits between ATU and ATT because the effect is not the same for everyone."}
[11]{.pb-val} | : The same six people, averaged. Solid cells are observable, dashed cells are counterfactual, and every causal quantity is a difference **down** a column. {#tbl-po} ::: The table is read in three directions, and each direction asks a different question: - **Down a column** — the same people under two regimes. This is a causal contrast. $69 - 55 = 14$ is {{< term att >}}, $43 - 35 = 8$ is {{< term atu >}}, and over both groups $56 - 45 = 11$ is {{< term ate >}}. - **Across the $Y(0)$ row** — different people under the *same* regime. Nothing causal is happening: $55 - 35 = 20$ is how far apart the two groups sit before college is even on the table. - **Across the two solid cells** — the only comparison the data supports, and the one that mixes the first two together. That third reading is the naive estimator, and it is what a spreadsheet gives you: $$ \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T = 0]}_{\text{naive}} \;=\; 69 - 35 \;=\; 34. $$ Read causally it says college is worth 34. The true average effect is 11. The naive number overstates it threefold, and the excess is not an arithmetic slip — it is the 20 sitting in the $Y(0)$ row, the gap that would have been there had nobody gone to college at all. Worth noting what the plain average $\mathbb{E}[Y] = 52$ contributes here: nothing. It averages people living under two different regimes, so it answers no causal question at all. ::: {.recall} In the potential-outcomes table a **causal** contrast is read *down a column* — the same people under two regimes. The naive contrast is read *across the two observed cells* — different people under different regimes. Every method in this course is a way of filling in one counterfactual cell so that a column can be read. ::: ### Where the bias comes from The naive difference in means decomposes into two parts. This identity is the center of the chapter [@angrist2009; @facure2022]: $$ \begin{aligned} & \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid T=0]}_{\text{what the data gives you}} \\[1.6em] ={} & \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid T=1]}_{\text{ATT — what you wanted}} \\[1.6em] +{} & \underbrace{\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=1] - \mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=0]}_{\text{selection bias}} \end{aligned} $$ The second term is how much the groups would have differed **with no treatment at all**. It is unobservable, because it is made of counterfactuals. On the six people of @tbl-po the identity reads $34 = 14 + 20$: of the 34 the spreadsheet reports, 14 is college and 20 is who went. What the identity separates is two different comparisons — the one we want and the one the data offers (@fig-causation-association). ::: {#fig-causation-association} {{< diagram causation-vs-association >}} **Causation** contrasts the whole population with itself under two regimes: no unit sits on only one side, and no dataset contains this comparison. **Association** contrasts the treated part with the untreated part: two different sets of units, and the comparison every dataset hands you for free. Selection bias is the distance between the two. Redrawn after @hernan2020. ::: ::: {.recall} Naive difference = ATT + {{< term selection-bias >}}. Selection bias is not noise and not sampling error: it does not shrink as the sample grows. More data makes a wrong answer more precise, not more correct. ::: ### What has to be assumed ::: {.assumption name="Ignorability"} $$(Y(0), Y(1)) \perp T \mid X$$ Within each level of the covariates $X$, treatment is as good as randomly assigned. In a {{< term rct >}} this holds by construction, because a coin does the assigning. In observational data it is an untestable assumption: the data can neither confirm nor refute it, only subject-matter knowledge can argue for it. ::: ::: {.assumption name="Positivity"} $$0 < P(T = 1 \mid X = x) < 1 \quad \text{for all } x$$ Every unit has a nonzero chance of landing in either group. If at some $x$ everyone is treated or nobody is, there is no counterfactual available there — and no method repairs that. ::: ::: {.assumption name="SUTVA"} A unit's outcome does not depend on what was assigned to other units, and the treatment exists in a single version. Violated by network effects and by marketplaces, where units compete for a shared resource. ::: ## [4]{.chapter-step} Verify with code {#sec-verification} Let us check the identity from step 3 on a simulation where the truth is known by construction. Two datasets with the **same** true effect $\tau = 2$: in the first, assignment is random; in the second, a confounder drives it. ::: {#cell-simulate .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} TRUE_ATE = 2.0 rct = randomized_trial(n=4000, ate=TRUE_ATE, seed=7) obs = confounded(n=4000, ate=TRUE_ATE, confounding=3.0, seed=7) pd.DataFrame( { "design": ["Randomized", "Confounded"], "true ATE": [true_ate(rct), true_ate(obs)], "true ATT": [true_att(rct), true_att(obs)], "naive difference": [naive_diff(rct), naive_diff(obs)], "bias": [naive_diff(rct) - true_ate(rct), naive_diff(obs) - true_ate(obs)], } ).round(3) ``` ::: {#simulate .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
design true ATE true ATT naive difference bias
0 Randomized 2.0 2.0 2.021 0.021
1 Confounded 2.0 2.0 6.165 4.165
``` ::: ::: The true effect is 2 in both designs. The naive difference recovers it in the first and lands near 6 in the second — three times the truth, with the bias term alone twice the size of the real effect. The difference is not in the data and not in the sample size; it is entirely in the **assignment mechanism**. Let us see where the bias came from. The confounder $x$ pushes both the probability of treatment and the outcome itself, so the groups separate along $x$ before treatment has done anything at all. ::: {#cell-fig-confounding .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} obs_plot = obs.assign(group=np.where(obs["t"] == 1, "Treated", "Control")) fig = px.scatter( obs_plot, x="x", y="y", color="group", opacity=0.45, # Plotly switches to WebGL above ~1000 points on its own. SVG keeps the # chart working without a GPU and keeps it recolorable on theme toggle. render_mode="svg", color_discrete_map={"Control": C.control, "Treated": C.treated}, labels={"x": "Confounder x", "y": "Observed outcome y"}, ) fig.update_traces(marker=dict(size=5, line=dict(width=0))) apply_theme(fig) fig.update_layout(height=420) fig ``` ::: {#fig-confounding .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` The confounder pulls the groups apart along x. The vertical gap between the clouds is the effect and the bias added together, and no amount of looking separates them. ::: ::: Now the same thing in terms of the identity. Split the naive difference into ATT and selection bias — in a simulation both parts are computable, because the potential outcomes are known. ::: {#cell-fig-decomposition .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} parts = {"Randomized": decompose(rct), "Confounded": decompose(obs)} designs = list(parts) fig = go.Figure() fig.add_bar( name="ATT — the causal effect", x=designs, y=[parts[d]["att"] for d in designs], marker_color=C.treated, ) fig.add_bar( name="Selection bias", x=designs, y=[parts[d]["bias"] for d in designs], marker_color=C.bias, ) fig.update_layout( barmode="relative", height=400, yaxis_title="Contribution to the naive difference", ) truth_line(fig, y=TRUE_ATE, label="True ATE = 2") apply_theme(fig) fig ``` ::: {#fig-decomposition .cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` Decomposition of the naive difference. Under randomization the selection-bias segment is zero by construction, so the naive estimate lands on the truth. ::: ::: The segments add up to exactly the naive difference. In the randomized design the second segment is degenerate — the coin knows nothing about the potential outcomes, so $\mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=1] = \mathbb{E}[Y(0) \mid T=0]$. ::: {.quiz question="The sample grows from 4,000 to 400,000 observations. What happens to the bias in the second design?"} Nothing. Selection bias is a property of the **assignment mechanism**, not of the sample size. Only precision improves: the confidence interval tightens around the very same wrong number. This is what separates bias from random error, and it is why "we have millions of rows" is not an argument in a causal question. ::: ## [5]{.chapter-step} Explorable {#sec-explorable} The table above shows two points: confounding present, confounding absent. The interesting part is the whole transition between them. → [**Bias from confounding**](/explorables/confounding-bias.qmd) — move a slider to vary the confounder's strength from zero and watch the truth and the naive estimate separate. At zero the design degenerates into a randomized experiment. ## [6]{.chapter-step} When it breaks {#sec-failure} | What happens | Why it hurts | Signal in the data | |---|---|---| | The driver of selection is unobserved | Controlling for covariates cannot help — there is nothing to control | None. The data looks fine | | Positivity is violated | At some $x$ there is no counterfactual at all | Propensity estimates pile up near 0 or 1 | | SUTVA is violated | The control group is contaminated by the treatment | Network structure, shared resource, marketplace | | Effect is heterogeneous but ATE is reported | The number is right, the decision is wrong | ATT diverges noticeably from ATE | | Controlling for a collider | Adding a control **creates** bias | The estimate moves when a "sensible" variable is added | The last row is the treacherous one. The instinct that "more controls cannot hurt" is wrong: controlling for a variable that is a consequence of both treatment and outcome opens a path that did not exist. Covered in the chapter on DAGs. ::: {.quiz question="Why not simply put every available variable into the regression?"} Because variables come in kinds that must be handled differently. Controlling for a {{< term confounder >}} removes bias; controlling for a collider creates it. The data cannot tell them apart — only an assumed causal structure can. The consequence: choosing controls is a decision made **before** looking at the data, on the basis of subject-matter knowledge. ::: ## [7]{.chapter-step} In my own words {#sec-summary} Causal inference starts by admitting the necessary data does not exist and never will. Every unit has two potential outcomes, exactly one is observed, so the individual effect is unavailable in principle. Averages rescue us — but only if we know how treatment was assigned. A naive difference in means always equals the real effect plus selection bias. Randomization zeroes the second term by construction, and that single property is its entire value. Everything else in the course is a way to zero out selection bias where randomization is impossible. Each method buys that with an assumption the data cannot check. ::: {.recall} Methods of causal inference differ less in their mathematics than in **which untestable assumption** they demand in exchange for randomization. Judge a method by how plausible its assumption is in the problem at hand, not by how sophisticated its machinery looks. :::
